strengths: The paper explores a genuinely under-explored direction in continual learning: rather than preventing representation drift, it learns per-task 'rectifier' units that map drifted representations back to past task domains, separating plasticity from stability. This is a fresh conceptual framing with clear novelty relative to rehearsal, regularization, and expansion methods.

The method is simple and modular (a weak feature extractor, compress and combine layers), and the authors provide useful disambiguation from closely related paradigms (network expansion, buffer-based replay), including an empirical check that naively training standalone weak extractors performs poorly (<53% on CIFAR100).

The evaluation covers three standard benchmarks (S-CIFAR10, S-CIFAR100, S-TinyImg), both task- and class-incremental protocols, multiple buffer sizes, ablations of the loss components (α, τ), a parameter-growth analysis, PCA visualizations of rectification quality, and hyperparameter details in the appendix.

The limitations section is candid: it acknowledges per-task parameter overhead, costly inference chains, the dependence on task t−1 data, and the weakness of the ensemble-based class-incremental solution.
The approach is architecturally orthogonal and can be combined with existing CL pipelines, which increases its potential usefulness.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is a central concern. ILR's reported superiority on S-CIFAR100 and S-TinyImg holds only when its alignment set contains 5000 samples from the previous task, while rehearsal baselines are limited to 500–1000 total buffered samples across all tasks. With matched 500/1000-sample alignment sets, ILR generally loses to DER++, ER-ACE, and TAMiL. The appendix even concedes this is 'not a fair comparison', which undercuts the paper's headline empirical claim that ILR 'outperforms all the baselines'.

Class-incremental performance is below all rehearsal baselines at matched budgets (42.53 vs 46.96 for DER++ at |S|=1000) and only approaches them with the oversized 5000-sample set; the ensemble inference is ad hoc and acknowledged to be fragile.

The 'data-free' narrative is weakened by the generative option: it requires a ~95M-parameter BigGAN per task (vs. a 11.27M base model), which is a very large memory cost, and this option is only evaluated on one dataset. The 'keep t−1 data' variants also undermine the claimed advantage over replay methods (task t−1 data is retained, just discarded one task later).

There is no analysis of error compounding along the rectifier chain, which is the method's core mechanism and grows linearly with the number of tasks; quantitative representation-alignment metrics are missing (only qualitative PCA plots). The cosine-term ablation shows near-zero benefit on S-TinyImg (72.07 vs 72.50), weakening the claimed novelty of the alignment loss.

The manuscript has numerous inconsistencies that impede reliability: the method is called 'LRB' in Tables 3–4; the appendix describes S-TinyImg as 10 tasks with 1,100,000 images while the main text uses 20 tasks; the current-task-data option in Section 4.3 is written as D_train_{t-1}; typos throughout ('Distiction', 'infernece', 'recevies', 'CSL-ER'); and dataset statistics (60000 images for CIFAR) are stated loosely. No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility for a method with several unspecified design choices (rectifier dimensions, distillation details of h_t).

The evaluation is limited to small-scale image classification with task-identity available at inference (task-incremental) and short task sequences (5–20 tasks); scalability of the chain mechanism beyond this regime remains untested.

strengths: The core idea—learning lightweight backward 'rectifier' units that map current representations back to previous-task representation spaces rather than preventing representation drift—is an interesting and somewhat underexplored angle in continual learning, and the paper frames it clearly as an alternative to rehearsal, regularization, and expansion approaches.

The experimental coverage is reasonably broad: three standard benchmarks (S-CIFAR10, S-CIFAR100, S-TinyImg), both task- and class-incremental protocols, multiple alignment-set options (previous-task data, current-task data, GAN-generated data), an ablation of the alignment loss (τ, α), parameter-growth accounting (Table 4), and a PCA visualization of rectifier quality (Figure 3).
The limitations section (Section 5) is candid about inference-chain overhead, reliance on task t−1 data, and the weakness of the ensemble solution for class-incremental inference.
Hyperparameter search ranges and final hyperparameters are reported in the appendix, and implementation builds on established repositories (Mammoth, TAMiL, CLS-ER).
weaknesses: The central 'data-free / no replay buffer' framing is misleading. ILR's best results (Table 1: |St| = 5000) require storing 5,000 samples of task t−1 data—10× the replay budget given to ER/DER++/ER-ACE (500–1,000 total). The paper even acknowledges this comparison 'is not fair' in Appendix A.1, yet the abstract and Table 1 present ILR 'outperforming all baselines' under this asymmetric memory regime, and the conclusion claims ILR 'requires neither a replay buffer nor intricate training modifications.' This materially undermines the headline claims.

The class-incremental results (Table 2) do not support the 'comparable performance' claim: ILR with |St|=1000 achieves 42.53 vs. DER++ 46.96 with a 10× smaller buffer, and even |St|=5000 (48.90) trails TAMiL (51.83) and CLS-ER (51.13). The simple ensemble inference is acknowledged to be unreliable, so the CIL extension is largely a proof-of-concept.

Limited originality: the mechanism is essentially a per-task backward adapter/distillation mapping with a weak feature extractor, closely resembling Progressive Networks-style lateral mappings and knowledge-distillation-into-auxiliary-network ideas; the paper's differentiation from network expansion (Section 3.2.2, and the <53% ablation) is asserted more than rigorously analyzed.

Notation and naming are inconsistent and error-prone: 'LRB' appears in Sections 3.1.2 and 4.4 and Table 4 without ever being defined; 'Distiction,' 'recevies,' 'infernece,' and other typos recur; the alignment-set description alternates between D_t and D_{t−1} in Table 3's caption discussion ('the current task's training data D^train_{t−1}').

The appendix contradicts the main text on experimental setup: Section 4.1 states S-TinyImg uses 20 tasks with 20 classes, while Appendix A.2 says 10 tasks; image counts ('1100000 64×64 images with 100000 training images') are internally inconsistent. These inconsistencies raise reproducibility and accuracy concerns.

No code release is mentioned, and key details affecting reproduction (how f_{t−1} is stored/frozen across the chain, compute cost of inference chains, forgetting metrics beyond average accuracy, error accumulation over the rectifier chain) are not quantified.

The task-incremental protocol already yields near-saturated baseline results on S-CIFAR10 (several methods >95%), making the TIL comparison on that dataset low-information; and ILR still trails CLS-ER there even with a 5,000-sample alignment set (94.84 vs 96.05).

The strongest configuration is essentially 'rehearsal of the previous task with a bigger buffer plus a learned mapping,' which weakens the paper's positioning as a genuinely new CL direction distinct from replay-based methods.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: rather than preventing forgetting during training, ILR lets the model forget and then 'recalls' old-task representations at inference via a chain of lightweight rectifier units. This reframing of the stability-plasticity trade-off is fresh and could inspire follow-up work.

The method is modular and practical: it does not modify the new task's training procedure, so it can in principle be bolted onto existing CL pipelines, and parameter growth (Table 4) is modest compared to TAMiL and CLS-ER.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation: three standard benchmarks (S-CIFAR10, S-CIFAR100, S-TinyImg), multiple buffer/alignment-set sizes, comparison against a representative set of baselines (EWC, LwF, ER, AGEM, DER++, ER-ACE, TAMiL, CLS-ER), an ablation of the loss components (Table 5), a study of alignment-set choices including a generative option (Table 3), and a PCA-based qualitative analysis of rectifier quality (Figure 3).

Hyperparameter search and implementation details are documented in the appendix (grid search ranges, optimizers, architectures, GAN training details), and the limitations section is candid about inference-chain cost, reliance on task t-1 data, and the weakness of the class-incremental ensemble solution.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is questionable. ILR's best results use an alignment set of 5,000 samples from task t-1, whereas the strongest rehearsal baselines use buffers of only 500-1,000 samples. At matched |St|=1,000, ILR does not consistently outperform CLS-ER and TAMiL (e.g., 78.53 vs 79.36 on S-CIFAR100; 66.79 vs 70.89 on S-TinyImg). Additionally, the task-t alignment option requires keeping a full copy of the previous feature extractor f_{t-1}, and it is unclear whether this ~11M-parameter cost is included in the memory accounting of Table 4.

Class-incremental results are notably weaker than task-incremental ones (Table 2: 42.53-48.90 vs 46.96-51.83 for baselines), and the proposed remedy is a simple softmax-averaging ensemble. Since class-incremental learning is the practically harder and more commonly studied setting, the method's applicability there remains underdeveloped.

Inference cost of the rectifier chain grows linearly with the number of tasks (each rectifier includes a forward pass through a weak feature extractor), but only parameter counts are analyzed; a latency/FLOPs comparison against baselines is missing.

Presentation and consistency issues undermine confidence: the method is referred to as both 'ILR' and 'LRB' in the same section (Section 3.1.2 and Table 4); the appendix describes S-TinyImg as 10 tasks while the main text says 20 tasks; numerous typos ('Distiction', 'recevies', 'infernece'); and no code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned.

Evaluation is limited to small-scale benchmarks (CIFAR/Tiny ImageNet with ResNet18). No experiments with pre-trained backbones or larger-scale streams, which are increasingly standard in the CL literature, and no significance testing beyond reported standard deviations.

The claimed advantage of being 'data-free' is overstated: the best configuration requires retaining 5,000 samples of the immediately preceding task, which is a form of rehearsal data, and the generative alternative requires a 95M-parameter BigGAN per task, which dwarfs the memory savings the method claims over replay buffers.

strengths: The core idea—learning lightweight retrospector modules that map current-task features backward to past task feature spaces—is a genuinely novel and interesting direction for continual learning that separates stability (post-hoc rectification) from plasticity (unconstrained new-task learning). This is an original reframing of how catastrophic forgetting can be mitigated.

The evaluation is fairly comprehensive: three standard benchmarks (S-CIFAR10, S-CIFAR100, S-TinyImg) under both TIL and CIL settings, comparisons against strong rehearsal baselines (ER, AGEM, DER++, ER-ACE, CLS-ER, TAMiL, ER-MKD) with EMA variants used for fairness, grid-searched hyperparameters, and 3 random seeds.

Notably, RFE (data-free) reaches 79.54% TIL accuracy on S-CIFAR100 and 69.66% on S-TinyImg, outperforming rehearsal methods with 500–1000 exemplars, and Fig. 4 shows robustness over long 20-task chains—an important stress test.

The paper supports the central claim mechanistically: PCA visualizations and RMSE measurements (Fig. 5, Fig. 6) directly show that rectified representations align with original representations, not just that downstream accuracy improves.

Good ablation coverage: alternative retrospector designs (MLP-Projection vs. gated design), end-to-end training, ViT backbone generalization, and honest overhead analysis (Tables 6–8, Sections B.1–B.2).

The limitations section is candid and specific: acknowledges that RFE does not beat SOTA on S-CIFAR10, that long chains incur inference cost, and that CIL currently requires task-identity inference or probability averaging.
weaknesses: The 'data-free' framing is somewhat overstated. RFE keeps the entire previous feature extractor f_{t-1} (plus a distilled auxiliary extractor h_t and a growing chain of retrospectors), giving it the largest training/inference parameter footprint among many compared methods (e.g., 23.76M params on S-CIFAR10 vs. 11.17M for buffer methods). Storing a full prior backbone is comparable in memory to storing a large exemplar buffer, and the paper's own Section B.2 concedes this (~14.36M vs. ~12.28M params). The memory/privacy trade-off story in Table 1 should be presented more carefully.

The distillation component (Eq. 7, alpha * LFE aligning f_t to f_{t-1}) is essentially Learning without Forgetting (Li & Hoiem, 2018), which the paper cites but does not position RFE against empirically. The related-work treatment of feature/distillation-based methods is thin, and the ablation isolating the contribution of the distillation term alpha versus the retrospector chain itself is missing—this weakens attribution of gains to the proposed retrospective mechanism.

CIL results are mixed and weaker than the abstract's framing suggests: on S-CIFAR100, RFE-P/RFE-B (45.85/46.01 at |B|=1000) are substantially below CLS-ER (56.18), and only on S-TinyImg do they lead. The simple softmax-averaging inference is acknowledged to be suboptimal, but then the strongest CIL claim rests on a single benchmark.

Composition of retrospector modules over many tasks raises an error-accumulation concern that is only empirically (not analytically) addressed; the per-hop rectification RMSE grows with chain length (Fig. 6), and there is no theoretical or controlled analysis of when chaining remains stable.

The retrospector depends on the current input x through the auxiliary extractor h_t at inference; this requires access to raw inputs at inference-time in a way that is somewhat in tension with the 'minimal modification, plug-in' narrative, and its sensitivity to the deliberately weak h_t design is not ablated (only justified qualitatively).

Presentation issues: the code availability URL is empty in the abstract; repeated typos ('RFE-P and RFE-P' in Section 4.2, 'Finetuning' row missing params in Tables 3/8); the paper incorrectly labels 'ER-MKD (Mallya & Lazebnik, 2017)' in Section B.6 (citation mismatch). The incomplete code link hurts reproducibility.

Comparison with non-rehearsal methods (Section B.6) relies on indirect cross-paper comparisons with different backbones (e.g., Kim et al. 2022 use a 2x-width ResNet18), which weakens the claim of matching SOTA non-rehearsal performance.

strengths: The paper explores a genuinely under-explored direction in continual learning: rather than preventing forgetting during training, it learns lightweight 'retrospector' modules that map features backward from the current task's representation space to past task spaces at inference time. This framing as a post-hoc rectification mechanism, largely decoupled from new-task training, is interesting and modular.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: three standard benchmarks (S-CIFAR10, S-CIFAR100, S-TinyImg), both task-incremental and class-incremental settings, buffer sizes of 500 and 1000, long-chaining experiments up to 20 tasks, a ViT-S/16 backbone experiment, ablations on alternative retrospector designs (Table 7), and time/space overhead analysis (Tables 6, B.2).

The authors appear to compare against strong EMA-enabled versions of TAMiL and CLS-ER rather than the weaker non-EMA versions often used in prior work, which is a point in favor of comparison fairness.

The paper includes an honest limitations section acknowledging inference-chain overhead, instability on fine-grained tasks (S-CIFAR10), and the reliance on task identity for reconstruction of the retrospector chain.

The auxiliary feature extractor is deliberately kept small and weak to demonstrate that gains come from retrospective rectification rather than auxiliary capacity, and the qualitative PCA/RMSE analysis (Fig. 5, Fig. 6) provides some direct evidence that the retrospector reverses representation drift.
weaknesses: The headline 'no past data' / 'data-free' claim is misleading. RFE (a) retains the entire previous task's feature extractor f_{t-1} (a full ResNet18, ~11M parameters), which doubles inference-time parameters (23.76M vs. 11.17M for baselines in Table 2), and (b) uses LwF-style distillation regularization (Eq. 7) on current-task data during training. Parameter memory is substituted for exemplar memory, and a substantial portion of the gains may come from the well-established distillation regularizer rather than the retrospector mechanism itself. There is no main-table ablation isolating the contribution of the retrospector chain with alpha = 0; the alpha=0 setting appears only in the qualitative Fig. 5.

The strong task-incremental results rely on task identity at test time to select the retrospector chain. The class-incremental solution is a simple softmax averaging over all domains, which the authors themselves admit is naive; on S-CIFAR100 CIL, RFE (43.63) and even RFE-B (46.01) clearly underperform CLS-ER (56.18). No S-CIFAR10 CIL results are reported, and the CIL story feels underdeveloped relative to the claims.

The method's core assumption — that feature drift between consecutive tasks can be inverted by a small gated linear/auxiliary module, and that this composes over a chain of up to 20 modules — is only justified empirically. There is no analysis of when rectification fails (e.g., large or non-linear drift, representation collapse), no theory, and the acknowledged S-CIFAR10 failure suggests fragile behavior that is not well characterized.

The claimed practical advantages over rehearsal are questionable. RFE-P stores raw samples of task t-1 (so the 'privacy' advantage over buffer methods is limited), and the memory accounting in B.2 conflates stored image bytes with network parameters to argue favorably for RFE. Meanwhile each retrospector adds 0.35M parameters and inference cost grows with the chain length.

Experiments are confined to small- and mid-scale benchmarks (CIFAR and Tiny ImageNet, ResNet18). Given the central claim of a 'new paradigm,' results at larger scale or on more realistic streams would be needed to establish significance.

Presentation has notable defects: the code availability line is empty ('Code is available at:'), there are typos ('sentation', 'RFE, RFE-P, RFE-P' in Sec. 4.2), Table 6 has missing/inconsistent entries, and the paper leans heavily on the supplementary material for key details (overhead, ablations, architecture generalization).

Originality is moderate rather than high: the mechanism combines ideas that individually exist — knowledge distillation from a previous model (LwF), auxiliary compact networks, and per-task added modules (a form of parameter growth). The novelty lies mainly in the composition and the backward-rectification framing, which is valuable but incremental.

strengths: The core idea of RFE is genuinely novel and well-motivated: instead of preventing representational drift during training (replay/regularization/isolation), RFE lets forgetting happen and then learns lightweight 'retrospector' modules that map the current feature space back to previous task domains. This separates stability from plasticity in a way that is distinct from parameter-isolation and expansion methods, and the paper clearly articulates this distinction.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough for a CL paper: three standard benchmarks (S-CIFAR10, S-CIFAR100, S-TinyImg), both task- and class-incremental settings, strong baselines including the stronger EMA versions of TAMiL and CLS-ER (rather than the weaker non-EMA versions often compared against), 3 seeds with standard deviations, and hyperparameter grid searches over all methods.

Useful ablations and analyses: alternative retrospector designs (MLP-Projection/Residual) in Table 7, end-to-end training variant, PCA/RMSE visualization of feature rectification (Fig. 5, Fig. 6), long-chaining experiments over 20 tasks (Fig. 4), ViT backbone generalization (Table 8), and time/space overhead reporting (Tables 2, 6).

The limitations section is honest and specific (linear overhead growth with task count, inference cost of long chains, weaker performance on S-CIFAR10, task-identity dependence for CIL), which aids reproducibility and follow-up work.

The 'weak' auxiliary feature extractor design choice is well-handled: deliberately using a low-capacity h_t supports the claim that performance comes from retrospective rectification rather than the auxiliary extractor itself.
weaknesses: Error accumulation along the retrospector chain is the central unaddressed risk. Composing t-1 sequential learned mappings compounds per-module approximation error, yet the paper provides no analysis or measurement of how rectification error propagates with chain length beyond descriptive RMSE matrices; there is no theory or systematic experiment (e.g., varying chain length with fixed task count) establishing when chaining remains stable. The 'principled alternative' claim in the abstract is therefore not fully supported.

The data-free framing is somewhat overstated. RFE retains the entire previous feature extractor f_{t-1} (~11M params) plus a per-task auxiliary extractor and retrospector, and it also uses distillation-style regularization (Eq. 7, LwF-like) during task training. The contribution of this distillation vs. the retrospector chain itself is not cleanly disentangled in the main results; the α=0 setting appears only in the visualization study, not in the headline accuracy tables.

Class-incremental results are mixed and weaken the significance claim: on S-CIFAR100 (Table 3), RFE-P/RFE-B (45.5-46.0) trail CLS-ER (50.7-56.2) by a clear margin, and the CIL inference scheme (averaging softmax probabilities across all N domain-reconstructed representations) scales linearly with task count and may suffer from overconfident classifiers, as the authors themselves concede. RFE is really a task-incremental method with a somewhat ad hoc CIL extension.

The assumption that current task data x ~ D_t^train can proxy for D_{t-1} when training the retrospector (data-free RFE) is plausible for similar tasks but is never analyzed for task distribution mismatch, which is exactly the regime where CL methods are most stressed.

The reported data-free RFE result on S-CIFAR10 (91.15) does not beat rehearsal baselines (CLS-ER 94.99 at |B|=500), and comparisons with non-rehearsal/parameter-isolation methods (HAT, Sup, HyperNet, PNN, PackNet) are conducted only indirectly through numbers imported from other papers under different backbones and buffer sizes, which is not an apples-to-apples comparison.

Presentation has notable rough edges: a duplicated 'RFE-P, RFE-P' typo in Section 4.2, an incomplete Testing row in Table 6 (values shown only for RFE variants), and the code URL is missing from the abstract, all of which reduce polish for a main-track submission.
